chapter: Pee Wee Russell and going solo
title: Declining a College Swing Band tour, then staying in Europe
summary: Haggart persuaded him to decline a tour offer, but at Rotterdam a Dutch promoter offered Festival money and Robert Masters began handling him as a soloist.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Then you were approached with this offer and --
And so I took the letter, it was an offer to do a tour with the College Swing Band, incidentally, I go out with them very soon and do a tour of Germany in October.

And they offered a tremendous amount of money, there was no jazz player getting that kind of money playing in a band, and then I wanted, I thought for some years, going all out and become just a soloist and not being in a band and not being regimented any more, although the World's Greatest Jazz Band was a great band because Bobby Haggart was a beautiful musician and arranger, he wrote for it, and Yank Lawson, who was the other leader, was very nice to me and it was quite a nice thing and you had these marvelous players in the band and they did the best work, around the world.

We never spent a winter in the north, it was either in the Islands, or Mexico or Hawaii, California, wherever, so anyway, I showed to the letter to Bob and Bob said, 'See, Bud, we're just about to make the turn into success, I wish you'd stay and turn it down.'
He said he wished that I would. Well,

I did, on the strength of what Hag said, he sort of persuaded me, I stayed on. I did turn it down, but then when we came to Europe the next time, I told Hag, 'Well, we have no work for a month, and look at the scene and see -- I will just stay over, I didn't say I was definitely going to stay and we're in the Rotterdam Airport and most of the guys in the band -- we had finished the tour in Holland and the guys are going back now to London and then the States, and I am just going to London, where I have been now for three and a half years.

And a Dutch impressario came running up to me, all out of breath before we went in to get on the plane and he said, 'Mr. Freeman, would you want to stay over here and do some work in Holland? There's a big festival coming up called the Brada Festival, and he offered me a tremendous amount of money for -- just to play one hour, and so the agent, Robert Masters, who was handling us on the road, said, 'My God, how are you that they would offer that kind of money, because he had never been in the solo field, he had always been in the band field, so on the strength of that again, I decided to stay and I asked Robert to handle me.

He had never handled a jazz soloist before and now he's handling a dozen people and he's a tremendous success and everybody's doing well and it appears that the jazz soloists are outdrawing many bands. You know, they go into a

small room and it's just fantastic, so as I say, I have been here three and a half years, and I have always wanted to live in England, always loved London, although London has changed a great deal in the last 16 years, and it's a fantastic life really, because -- I think I might have mentioned this earlier in the tapes, Helen, but I -- it takes me an hour to get to Holland, London is my base. It takes an hour to get to Switzerland, an hour to get to Germany.
